meta.title: Who really said “Niagara Falls: The First Great Disappointment in Married Life”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Oscar Wilde really did say it — in an 1883 lecture, at more length. Ann Landers circulated a different variant, the “second greatest disappointment,” in 1969.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Niagara Falls: The First Great Disappointment in Married Life'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilde’s own words: “the sight of the stupendous waterfall must be one of the earliest, if not the keenest, disappointments in American married life.”

answer.label: Not Ann Landers — it condenses Oscar Wilde
answer.sourceLine: Wilde said this, but not in these words. In his lecture Impressions of America — delivered at Wandsworth Town Hall on Monday 24 September 1883 and printed in 1906 — he said: “I was disappointed with Niagara—most people must be disappointed with Niagara. Every American bride is taken there, and the sight of the stupendous waterfall must be one of the earliest, if not the keenest, disappointments in American married life.” The headline-sized version is a later compression of that sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the joke’s drift and finds the sharper “second greatest disappointment” variant was not Wilde’s at all — and it is that variant, not this one, that Ann Landers put into circulation.

source.excerpt: I was disappointed with Niagara—most people must be disappointed with Niagara. Every American bride is taken there, and the sight of the stupendous waterfall must be one of the earliest, if not the keenest, disappointments in American married life. One sees it under bad conditions, very far away, the point of view not showing the splendour of the water.
trail: The primary text was read in full. Project Gutenberg’s edition of Impressions of America ↗ (Oscar Wilde, ed. Stuart Mason; Sunderland: Keystone Press, 1906) contains the Niagara passage verbatim, including the phrase “disappointments in American married life.”

The same volume’s editorial introduction supplies the occasion: Wilde “returned to England and immediately began ‘an all round lecturing tour,’ his first visit being to Wandsworth Town Hall on Monday, September 24th, when he delivered to an enthusiastic audience a lecture on his ‘Impressions of America,’ which is contained in the following pages.”

Quote Investigator ↗ dates newspaper paraphrases of the joke to 1883 — an August 1883 item reprinting the New York World has “the first disappointment in the married life of many Americans who spend their honeymoon there” — and concludes that the 1883 citations and the 1906 text “are all reasonable choices” for Wilde’s remark.

On the variant that is usually hung on Ann Landers, QI is explicit: the joke using “second greatest disappointment” “was not constructed by Wilde though QI thinks it was probably derived from his remark,” appearing anonymously in 1927 before later writers reassigned it.
Wikiquote’s Oscar Wilde page was checked and carries no Niagara line at all, so nothing here rests on it.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: About Oscar Wilde
author.bio: Oscar Fingal O’Fflahertie Wills Wilde toured the United States through 1882 on a lecture circuit built to publicise the Aesthetic movement, travelling from New York to the mining camps of Colorado. He turned the trip into a lecture of his own, Impressions of America, which he delivered around Britain from 1883 — a performance of practised astonishment at American scale, plumbing and self-belief. The Niagara line is one of its set pieces, and like most of his best remarks it was shortened by everyone who repeated it.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two different things get confused here: a real Wilde sentence that was trimmed, and a punchier variant that is not his.

items.why: The advice columnist is tied to the other version. QI ↗ records a 1969 Washington Post report of Ann Landers giving “Niagara Falls is the second greatest disappointment to every American bride,” and notes she said her readers had taught it to her. She is a conduit for a variant, not the author of this line.
The sentiment and the phrase “disappointments in American married life” are Wilde’s own, read here in the 1906 printed lecture ↗. What is not his is the compression into a slogan.

QI finds this form “was not constructed by Wilde though QI thinks it was probably derived from his remark.” Its earliest instance there is anonymous, in Anecdota Americana in 1927, decades after Wilde’s death in 1900.

misattribution.truthLine: Wilde made the joke, at length, in a lecture he gave in 1883. The one-line version belongs to whoever sharpened it — and the “second greatest” twist, the one Ann Landers passed along, is not Wilde’s at all.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Wilde’s American tour was a publicity exercise, and he repaid it with a lecture that made a running joke of American bigness — a country, he said, that “seems to try to bully one into a belief in its power by its impressive bigness.” Niagara was the perfect target: the one sight every honeymooning couple was obliged to admire.

The line survives because it is a small act of permission. It is still, a century and a half later, slightly rude to say that the famous thing was underwhelming, which is why the joke keeps being re-cut and re-assigned to whoever is currently allowed to be blunt — a Victorian aesthete, then an American agony aunt.
detailsBody: The drift is visible in the citations. In 1883 newspapers paraphrase Wilde loosely. In 1906 the lecture is printed and the long sentence is fixed on the page. In 1927 an anonymous joke book flips “first” to “second” — a cruder gag, and a better one for telling aloud. By 1969 Ann Landers is repeating that version and saying her readers gave it to her, and by 1977 a quotation dictionary has handed it back to Wilde, who never wrote it.
